title: Employment in High-AI-Exposure Occupations
description: Measured employment change in occupations classified as highly AI-exposed (top quartile by AI exposure indices). Most studies find near-zero aggregate displacement but a sharp age gradient: young workers (22-30) in AI-exposed roles show -5% to -13% declines across the US, Sweden, and the Netherlands, while older workers are stable or growing. Finland and Denmark report null results. Data points span both age-specific and all-worker measurements.

sources.title: The Potentially Large Effects of AI on Economic Growth
sources.excerpt: Two-thirds of US occupations are exposed to some degree of AI automation. Administrative and legal professions face the highest exposure rates at 46%.

sources.title: The economic potential of generative AI: The next productivity frontier
sources.excerpt: Banking, insurance, and capital markets could see up to 50% of current work activities automated. Legal research and contract review are among the most automatable tasks.

sources.title: GPTs are GPTs: An Early Look at the Labor Market Impact Potential of LLMs
sources.excerpt: ~80% of the US workforce could have at least 10% of their tasks affected by GPTs. Legal, accounting, and financial analysis are among the highest-exposure occupations.

sources.title: Elevating Human Potential: The AI Skills Revolution
sources.excerpt: top three uses of AI today. 51% Data analysis. 43% Fraud detection and security monitoring. 39% Human resources and recruiting processes

sources.title: Which jobs are most exposed to generative AI?
sources.excerpt: High-paid, white-collar occupations in business, finance, and law are among the most exposed to generative AI disruption.

sources.title: AI might not be coming for lawyers' jobs anytime soon
sources.excerpt: Despite early signs that AI is beginning to affect entry-level workers, labor statistics have yet to show lawyers being displaced. Law graduate employment in 2024 reached 93.4% — the highest rate on record.

sources.title: Tens of Thousands of White-Collar Jobs Are Disappearing as AI Starts to Bite
Strategies for Workforce Evolution
sources.excerpt: A Deloitte survey reveals how AI and human collaboration can help close talent gaps, speed upskilling, and transfer knowledge as demographic changes reshape the workforce.

sources.title: OECD Employment Outlook 2025: AI and High-Skill Occupations
sources.excerpt: Professional services occupations face the largest task-level AI exposure among high-income economies, with 18-25% of tasks fully automatable by current LLMs.

sources.title: JPMorgan Chase 2024 10-K — AI and Workforce
sources.excerpt: JPMorgan disclosed deploying LLM-based tools across legal, compliance, and research functions, with estimated productivity gains equivalent to 3,000+ full-time roles.

sources.title: EY Global — AI Transformation in Professional Services
sources.excerpt: EY invested $1.4B in AI, reporting that AI-assisted audit procedures now cover 40% of routine testing tasks previously performed by junior staff.

sources.title: 26% of Jobs Face Radical Transformation from AI, Indeed Finds
sources.excerpt: Indeed analysis finds 26% of jobs face radical transformation from AI. Paralegals face 80% automation risk by 2026. Legal research and contract review most affected.

sources.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Labor Market
sources.excerpt: Tasks with higher AI exposure subsequently experience reduced labor demand. 1 SD increase in AI exposure reduces relative demand for related skills by 2%.

sources.title: Technology and Labor Markets: Past, Present, and Future; Evidence from Two Centuries of Innovation
sources.excerpt: In sharp contrast to the past two centuries, AI will shift relative demand toward occupations with lower education, lower wages, and a greater share of male workers.

sources.title: Labor Demand in the Age of Generative AI: Early Evidence from the U.S. Job Posting Data
sources.excerpt: Job postings for high-AI-substitution occupations fell 18% relative to low-substitution roles by year three post-ChatGPT. This measures posting-level demand shifts in white-collar occupations.

sources.title: Experimental Evidence on the Productivity Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence
sources.excerpt: RCT: ChatGPT reduced task completion time by 40% and raised output quality by 18%. Low-ability workers benefited most, compressing the productivity distribution.

sources.title: Displacement or Complementarity? The Labor Market Impact of Generative AI
sources.excerpt: 24% decrease in AI-exposed skills required in highly automatable jobs, but 15% increase in AI-exposed skills for augmentation-prone professional roles.

sources.title: Is Generative AI a Job Killer? Evidence from the Freelance Market
sources.excerpt: High-skill freelancers disproportionately affected by AI — top performers were impacted most, contradicting conventional wisdom that expertise insulates workers.

sources.title: AI and jobs: A review of theory, estimates, and evidence
sources.excerpt: AI exposure measures converge toward high-wage jobs being most exposed; digital trace data show substitution already occurring in writing and translation.

sources.title: AI's Impact on Job Growth
sources.excerpt: Non-routine cognitive job workers now face rising unemployment risk, surpassing non-routine manual workers for the first time.

sources.title: Gartner Top Predictions 2025: 20% of Orgs Will Use AI to Flatten Structure by 2026
sources.excerpt: By 2026, 20% of organizations will use AI to flatten their organizational structure, eliminating more than half of current middle management positions in those organizations.

sources.title: How Will AI Affect the Global Workforce?
sources.excerpt: Only 2.5% of work tasks are currently at risk of direct displacement from AI. Remaining exposure is augmentation-oriented, boosting productivity without eliminating roles.

sources.title: AI Is Coming for Inefficiency, Not People
sources.excerpt: Less than 1% of announced layoffs in the first half of 2025 are attributable to productivity gains from AI; most (79%) have been unrelated to AI.

sources.title: AI Revolution: CFOs Forecast a Transformation in Finance Teams
sources.excerpt: 18% of CFOs have already eliminated roles due to AI. Of those, 88% of cuts were in accounting, 38% in FP&A, 33% in treasury. Finance teams are the earliest white-collar AI displacement.

sources.title: Companies Are Laying Off Workers Because of AI's Potential, Not Its Performance
sources.excerpt: 95% of generative AI projects have failed to deliver measurable returns (citing MIT). PwC: 56% of CEOs said AI failed to boost revenue or lower costs. Layoffs are anticipatory, not performance-driven.

sources.title: The Impact of AI on the Legal Profession: Evidence from ChatGPT
sources.excerpt: AI chatbots had no statistically significant impact on hours worked or wages earned for lawyers. Law graduate employment in 2024 reached 93.4% — the highest rate on record.

sources.title: Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier: Field Experimental Evidence of the Effects of AI on Knowledge Worker Productivity and Quality
sources.excerpt: RCT with 758 BCG consultants: for tasks within AI's capabilities, 12.2% more tasks completed, 25.1% faster, output rated 40% higher quality. For tasks outside AI's frontier, performance was 19pp worse.

sources.title: New Work, New World 2026: How AI is Reshaping Work
sources.excerpt: Education task exposure jumped from 11% to 49% — a 4.5x increase driven by multimodal AI, advanced reasoning, and agentic systems. Based on reassessment of 18,000 tasks across 1,000 O*NET occupations.

sources.title: Task-Specific Technical Change and Comparative Advantage
sources.excerpt: administrative occupations (e.g., financial clerks) see a large decline in employment, while science occupations (e.g., life scientists) expand

sources.title: Measuring US workers' capacity to adapt to AI-driven job displacement
sources.excerpt: Professional and managerial occupations (56.9 million workers) have relatively higher adaptive capacity on average (0.734) despite substantial exposure (0.400).

sources.title: AI and the Future of White-Collar Work: Expert Survey Results
sources.excerpt: the median expert predicted 2% growth in white-collar jobs between January 2025 and December 2030, compared to 6.8% pre-existing trend; one in four experts foreseeing net job losses

sources.title: Fault Lines
sources.excerpt: the jobs most vulnerable to AI are elsewhere—including executive assistants, editors, and interpreters/translators (where over 70% of their skills are exposed to AI).

sources.title: Claude Code 27: Research and Publishing Are Now Two Different Things
sources.excerpt: Project APE — Autonomous Policy Evaluation... has produced 204 papers — with 60 added in a single week... These are fully automated papers, like a version 1.0, with no human iteration whatsoever.

sources.title: How Well Does Agent Development Reflect Real-World Work?
sources.publisher: Carnegie Mellon / Stanford (Wang, Neubig, Fried, Yang et al.)
sources.excerpt: Management, Legal, and Architecture and Engineering exhibit high ratios of digital work (88%, 70%, and 71%, respectively). Management and Legal are sparsely covered by existing benchmarks (1.4%, 0.3% among all 19179 examples).

sources.title: State of IT jobs: AI sparks rapidly changing market for skills
sources.excerpt: 40% plan to reduce staff as skills become redundant

sources.title: Incorporating AI impacts in BLS employment projections: occupational case studies
sources.publisher: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (Monthly Labor Review)
sources.excerpt: Employment of personal financial advisors is projected to grow 17.1 percent from 2023 to 2033, much faster than average. Employment of paralegals and legal assistants is projected to grow only 1.2 percent, slower than the average for all occupations.

sources.title: Beyond Productivity: Measuring the Real Value of AI
sources.excerpt: In most organizations (89%), fewer than half of roles have been updated to reflect AI capabilities.

sources.title: Looking for the Ladder: Is AI Impacting Entry-Level Jobs?
sources.excerpt: There is no evidence that job postings for junior roles within occupations most exposed to AI have declined more than postings for senior positions. Postings for both levels of seniority have been falling roughly in parallel since their peak in Spring 2022, with the decline in junior positions stabilizing faster.

sources.title: Labor market impacts of AI: A new measure and early evidence
sources.excerpt: Workers in the most exposed professions are more likely to be older, female, more educated, and higher-paid. They earn 47% more, on average.

sources.title: Job Openings and Labor Turnover — December 2025
sources.excerpt: Professional & business services openings down 21.8% (-284,000). Financial activities openings down 25.1% (-86,000).

sources.title: How AI Is Turbocharging the War in Iran
sources.excerpt: The U.S. Army's 18th Airborne Corps, using software from data company Palantir Technologies in a continuing string of exercises dubbed Scarlet Dragon, matched its own record from Iraq as the military's most efficient targeting operation ever, according to Emelia Probasco, a senior fellow at Georgetown University's Center for Security and Emerging Technology. Thanks to AI, the corps achieved that with only 20 people, compared with more than 2,000 staffers employed in Iraq, she said.

sources.title: Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of AI
sources.publisher: Stanford Digital Economy Lab (Brynjolfsson, Chandar, Chen)
sources.excerpt: Workers aged 22 to 25 have experienced a 6% decline in employment from late 2022 to September 2025 in the most AI-exposed occupations, compared to a 6-9% increase for older workers.

sources.title: Agents, robots, and us: Skill partnerships in the age of AI
sources.publisher: McKinsey Global Institute (Yee, Madgavkar, Smit et al.)
sources.excerpt: Currently demonstrated technologies could automate activities accounting for about 57 percent of US work hours today. AI agents could perform tasks occupying 44 percent of US work hours, while robots could handle another 13 percent. Roles with the highest potential for automation make up about 40 percent of total jobs.

sources.title: AI-fueled layoffs are rising, but a great divide is emerging
sources.excerpt: Mustafa Suleyman, CEO of Microsoft AI, stated last month that he expects all white-collar work will be automated by AI within 18 months.

sources.title: Dalende werkgelegenheid onder Nederlandse jongeren die concurreren met GenAI
sources.excerpt: Zo lag het aantal openstaande vacatures in de meest vatbare beroepsgroepen in het tweede kwartaal van 2025 bijna 25 procent lager dan eind 2022. In de 102 overige beroepsgroepen daalde het aantal vacatures in dezelfde periode met minder dan 10 procent.

sources.title: Artificial Intelligence and White-Collar Work: Evidence from the Accounting Profession
sources.publisher: SSRN (Boke, De la Parra, Gallemore, Glaeser)
sources.excerpt: AI investment reduces accounting hiring but not work quality. 10 additional AI accounting roles associated with 49 fewer accounting-skill postings.

sources.title: GenAI and Seniority Composition
sources.excerpt: GenAI adopters cut junior hiring 22%; seniority composition shifts toward more experienced workers.

sources.title: Shifting Work Patterns with Generative AI
sources.publisher: NBER / AER: Insights (Dillon, Jaffe, Immorlica, Stanton)
sources.excerpt: In a field experiment across 66 firms and 7,137 knowledge workers, the 80% of treated workers who used the AI tool spent two fewer hours on email each week. We do not detect shifts in the quantity or composition of workers' tasks.

sources.title: How People Use ChatGPT
sources.publisher: NBER (Chatterji, Cunningham, Deming, Hitzig, Ong, Shan, Wadman)
sources.excerpt: By July 2025, 18 billion messages were being sent each week by 700 million users. 81% of work-related messages involve obtaining information or making decisions, not task automation.

sources.title: The Cybernetic Teammate: A Field Experiment on Generative AI Reshaping Teamwork and Expertise
sources.excerpt: In a pre-registered RCT with 776 P&G professionals, individuals with AI matched teams without AI (+0.37 SD improvement). AI broke professional silos.

sources.title: The Iceberg Index: Measuring Skills-centered Exposure in the AI Economy
sources.publisher: MIT / Oak Ridge National Laboratory (Project Iceberg)
sources.excerpt: Administrative and financial tasks where AI demonstrates capability span five times more wage value than visible tech disruption—and are geographically distributed across all states, not just coastal.

sources.title: How Adaptable Are American Workers to AI-Induced Job Displacement?
sources.excerpt: Professional and managerial occupations (56.9 million workers) have relatively higher adaptive capacity on average (0.734) despite substantial exposure (0.400), while administrative support occupations have lower adaptive capacity (0.360) combined with the highest AI exposure of any major occupation group (0.525).

sources.title: Artificial Intelligence, Productivity, and the Workforce: Evidence from Corporate Executives
sources.publisher: Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta / Duke University (Baslandze et al.)
sources.excerpt: CFOs expect routine clerical employment share to decline by 0.76pp in 2026 and 2.19pp by 2028, with partially offsetting increases in skilled-technical roles (+0.62pp in 2026). Business/financial operations NEI of 0.829 indicates roughly balanced replacement and enhancement.

sources.title: Same Storm, Different Boats: Generative AI and the Age Gradient in Hiring
sources.publisher: RATIO Institute / Örebro University (Lodefalk, Löthman, Koch, Engberg)
sources.excerpt: An event study documents an accelerating decline in employment of 22–25-year-olds in high-AI-exposure occupations, reaching 5.5 per cent by early 2025 relative to less exposed occupations within the same employers, while employment of workers over 50 rose by 1.3 per cent.

sources.title: The Projected Impact of Generative AI on Future Productivity Growth
sources.excerpt: Roughly 10% of US work affected in the short run; AI will increase productivity and GDP by 1.5% by 2035. Jobs that AI can completely replace saw 0.75% employment fall 2021-2024.

sources.title: Bridging Skill Gaps for the Future: New Jobs Creation in the AI Age
sources.excerpt: Employment 3.6% lower in AI-vulnerable occupations in regions with high AI-skill demand after 5 years; geographic divergence driven by skill concentration.

sources.title: AI Exposure and Unemployment Risk
sources.excerpt: Unemployment risk in AI-exposed occupations rose beginning early 2022; graduates with AI-exposed curricula have higher first-job pay and shorter job searches post-ChatGPT.

sources.title: AI's Use of Knowledge in Society
sources.excerpt: The framework yields several predictions: larger average firm size, greater industry concentration, and reduced local managerial autonomy.

sources.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Labor Market
sources.excerpt: Most adversely impacted occupations (business, financial, engineering) experienced a decline of 2% to 2.5% over a five-year period. Reduced demand in exposed occupations is offset by productivity-driven increases in labor demand at AI-adopting firms.

sources.title: Displacement or Complementarity? The Labor Market Impact of Generative AI
sources.excerpt: 24% decrease in generative AI-exposed skills per firm per quarter in top-quartile automation-exposed jobs. 15% increase in AI-exposed skills for augmentation-prone jobs. Augmentation-prone job postings increased 22% per quarter per firm.
